# Kisāgotamītherīgāthā (Thig 10.1)

**ID:** Thig 10.1
**Section:** Therīgāthā (thig)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Kisāgotamītherīgāthā

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kisāgotamītherīgāthā* (Thig 10.1) is a canonical poem preserved in the *Therīgāthā* ("Verses of Senior Nuns") of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. Modern English translations of the text include versions by Bhikkhu Sujato and Ayya Soma [SuttaCentral].

In these verses, the elder nun (*therī*) Kisāgotamī reflects upon the intrinsic misery and trials of female embodiment (*dukkho itthibhāvo*), noting that the Buddha—the "trainer of persons to be tamed" (*purisadammasārathī*)—declared womanhood to be suffering [Gutschow 2004; Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Collett 2014]. Her verses describe the severe physical and emotional ordeals experienced by women, including the grief of co-wives, the perils of obstructed childbirth where both mother and infant face destruction, and the desperation that drives delicate women to cut their throats or ingest poison [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Collett 2014]. The poem concludes on an exultant declaration of spiritual victory, proclaiming the development of the Noble Eightfold Path, the realization of Nibbāna by looking into the "mirror of the Dhamma," and full release with the burden laid down and the dart of suffering extracted [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

Unlike later narrative traditions in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and non-Pali Buddhist literature that famously associate Kisāgotamī with the parable of searching for a mustard seed from a house untouched by death, her canonical verses in the *Therīgāthā* focus directly on the trauma of female suffering and the achievement of awakening [Norman; Appleton 2010; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. In Pali exegetical literature, the text is cited and expounded in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, which shares extensive matching passages with these verses [DharmaNexus]. Text-reuse algorithms also indicate isolated cross-language phrase correspondences in the Tibetan translation of the *Ārya-sarvapuṇyasamuccayasamādhi-sūtra* [DharmaNexus].
